indexing.note: chained CPI-U per IRC 1(f), at most 4% a year, rounded to $10 (S.C. Code 12-6-520)

not_modelled.what: Surviving spouse retirement deduction (line p-3): 3,000 or 10,000 of a deceased spouse's retirement income, by the age the deceased spouse would have reached, in addition to the survivor's own deduction.
Surviving spouse military retirement deduction (line p-6): all military retirement and dependent indemnity compensation received for a deceased spouse's service.
Military retirement for Reserve or National Guard inactive service: the inactive share is excluded on line v (in practice already deducted in full by the military retirement deduction).
Total and permanent disability retirement income is deducted in full (line g).
Dependent exemption of 4,930 for each dependent, and another 4,930 for each dependent under age 6.
Two Wage Earner Credit: married couples filing jointly where both spouses have earned income get .007 of the lower earner's qualified earned income, up to 350.
Interest on US savings bonds, treasury notes and bills is subtracted (line m).
National Guard and Reserve drill and annual training pay is subtracted (line n).

approximations.what: The bracket starts 3,560 and 17,840 are derived from the printed tax table and the 6%-minus-642 formula; the table fixes them only to 3,559-3,566 and 17,818-17,857. Tax below 100,000 is figured on the exact income, where the booklet uses the table row's midpoint.
approximations.size: At most 3 dollars a year (6% of half a 100-dollar table row), plus well under 1 dollar from the threshold choice.

approximations.what: The booklet stacks the age 65 deduction on the retirement deduction (15,000 less the retirement and military deductions taken). The projection puts the 65-or-older retirement deduction and the age 65 deduction in one best_of_group, with the age 65 cap reduced by military retirement. For a person 65 or older this gives the same total as the worksheets, the larger of 15,000 and the military retirement income (Examples 1-5), whenever the person's income covers it.
approximations.size: None when the person's income is at least the deduction; otherwise state taxable income is zero either way.

approximations.what: Roth conversions are left out of the retirement deduction's covers (covers_unclear in the record). If South Carolina counts them, this overstates tax for a person under 65 converting with less than 3,000 of other retirement income.
approximations.size: At most 6% of 3,000 = 180 a person a year; none for a person 65 or older, whose age 65 deduction covers any income.

approximations.what: Retirement income that drew a federal premature withdrawal penalty does not qualify for the retirement deduction; the projection allows it.
approximations.size: At most 6% of 3,000 = 180 a person a year, only in years with penalised early withdrawals.

approximations.what: The retirement deduction is limited to the original owner's own plan; inherited IRA and beneficiary distributions (other than a surviving spouse's, not modelled) do not qualify, but the projection cannot tell them apart.
approximations.size: At most 6% of 3,000 = 180 a person a year under 65; none at 65 or older if the age 65 deduction is otherwise unused.

approximations.what: The 44% deduction applies to net capital gain (net long-term gain less net short-term loss); the projection applies it to long-term gains without netting short-term losses.
approximations.size: 6% x 44% = 2.64% of any short-term loss netted against long-term gains.

approximations.what: All municipal bond interest is treated as from other states (added back and taxed); South Carolina's own bonds are not added back.
Interest on US Treasury obligations is taxed (the projection cannot tell it from other interest).
South Carolina starts from federal taxable income; a household that itemizes and deducts state income tax must add back part of it (line a), which is not modelled.
approximations.size: 6% of the add-back, at most the itemized deductions above the federal standard deduction.
